steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Many robotics researchers have long had the dream of building mobile robots that can reach as many places as possible. And autonomous mobile robots have in fact gone into remote deserts for scientific exploration, explored extraterrestrial planets to look for signs of life, and helped with search and rescue missions in environments that are hazardous or difficult to reach.

One thrust in this research area is developing ground robots that can navigate vertically challenging terrain (e.g., steep slopes, rocky outcroppings, and uneven surfaces). It is challenging to get reliable and robust mobility in these environments, because the terrain is intricate, the vehicle-terrain interactions are complex, gravity has an adverse impact, the vehicle chassis can deform, and the traction between the wheels and the terrain varies. Even with these difficulties, this kind of mobility has been made possible, mainly through advances in hardware, like developing specialized robot platforms and using new materials. These robots can climb walls, scale cliffs, and traverse rough terrain easily, so they are suitable for a wide range of real-world applications.

- Limitation
  - most ground robots still conventional wheeled, mostly flat surfaces
  - navigation divides planar workspace into free space (traversable) / obstacles (non-traversable) -> less reachability, esp. outdoor off-road, vertical protrusions
  - our aim: expand mobility of widely available wheeled platforms into terrain otherwise obstacles or needing special hardware
  - note: irregular complex obstacles, much harder than non-flat ground
- Contributions
  - open-source Verti-Wheelers (two platforms), representative; hypothesis (Fig. 1)
  - public datasets for data-driven approaches (analytical models hard)
  - three algorithms: open-loop, classical rule-based, end-to-end learning; baselines
  - experiments indoor testbed + outdoor; confirm hypothesis; future directions
  - no existing work on this with conventional wheeled robots in real world

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Many robotics researchers have long had the dream of building mobile robots that can reach as many places as possible. And autonomous mobile robots have in fact gone into remote deserts for scientific exploration, explored extraterrestrial planets to look for signs of life, and helped with search and rescue missions in environments that are hazardous or difficult to reach.

One thrust in this research area is developing ground robots that can navigate vertically challenging terrain (e.g., steep slopes, rocky outcroppings, and uneven surfaces). It is challenging to get reliable and robust mobility in these environments, because the terrain is intricate, the vehicle-terrain interactions are complex, gravity has an adverse impact, the vehicle chassis can deform, and the traction between the wheels and the terrain varies. Even with these difficulties, this kind of mobility has been made possible, mainly through advances in hardware, like developing specialized robot platforms and using new materials. These robots can climb walls, scale cliffs, and traverse rough terrain easily, so they are suitable for a wide range of real-world applications.

But even with these hardware advances, most of the ground robots that are currently available are still conventional wheeled platforms, and their mobility is mostly limited to flat surfaces. Most existing autonomous navigation systems for wheeled robots just divide their workspaces, which are presumed to be planar, into free spaces (traversable) or obstacles (non-traversable). This reduces the reachability of these robots in the real world a lot, especially in outdoor off-road environments where vertical protrusions from the ground are not uncommon. Our work is motivated by these limitations. We aim to expand the mobility of these widely available wheeled robot platforms so they can go into vertically challenging environments that would otherwise be seen as obstacles (non-traversable) or would need specialized hardware. Note that the vertically challenging terrain we want to conquer requires driving wheeled robots over irregular and complex obstacles, so it is much more difficult than just driving on non-flat environments.

For this, first we present an open-source design of two wheeled robot platforms, the Verti-Wheelers, which represent most existing conventional ground mobile robot platforms, and we hypothesize that conventional wheeled robots can also navigate many vertically challenging terrain that are normally considered non-traversable obstacles (Fig. 1). Second, since it is difficult to create accurate analytical models for this problem, we collect datasets and make them publicly available to help data-driven approaches. Third, we present three algorithms for autonomously driving wheeled robots over vertically challenging terrain: an open-loop, a classical rule-based, and an end-to-end learning-based approach, and they can be used as baselines to benchmark future research. We give extensive experimental results of all three algorithms in an indoor controlled testbed and in outdoor natural environments, we confirm our hypothesis, and we point out future research directions for wheeled mobility on vertically challenging terrain. As far as we know, no existing work has tackled vertically challenging terrain with conventional wheeled robots in the real world.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Building mobile robots that can reach as many places as possible has long been a dream for many robotics researchers. Indeed, autonomous mobile robots have ventured into remote deserts for scientific exploration [1], explored extraterrestrial planets to look for signs of life [2,3], and assisted with search and rescue missions in hazardous or difficult-to-reach environments [4,5,6,7].

One particular thrust in this research area is the development of ground robots capable of navigating vertically challenging terrain (e.g., steep slopes, rocky outcroppings, and uneven surfaces) [8,9,10]. Achieving reliable and robust mobility in these environments is challenging due to the intricate nature of the terrain, complex vehicle-terrain interactions, the adverse impact of gravity, potential deformation of the vehicle chassis, and varying traction between the wheels and the terrain. Despite these difficulties, such mobility has been made possible mainly through hardware advances, including specialized robot platforms [4,10,11,3,12] and new materials [13]. These robots can climb walls [13], scale cliffs [10], and traverse rough terrain with ease [11,12], which makes them suitable for a wide range of real-world applications.

However, despite these hardware advances, the vast majority of currently available ground robots are still conventional wheeled platforms whose mobility is mostly limited to flat surfaces. Most existing autonomous navigation systems for wheeled robots simply divide their presumably planar workspaces into free spaces (traversable) and obstacles (non-traversable), which significantly reduces these robots' reachability in the real world, especially in outdoor off-road environments where vertical protrusions from the ground are not uncommon. Motivated by these limitations, our work aims to expand the mobility of widely available wheeled robot platforms so that they can venture into vertically challenging environments that would otherwise be deemed obstacles (non-traversable) or require specialized hardware. Note that the vertically challenging terrain we are interested in requires driving wheeled robots over irregular and complex obstacles, and is therefore much more difficult than simply driving in non-flat environments.

To this end, we first present an open-source design of two wheeled robot platforms, the Verti-Wheelers, which are representative of most existing conventional ground mobile robot platforms, and we hypothesize that conventional wheeled robots can also navigate many vertically challenging terrain normally considered non-traversable obstacles (Fig. 1). Second, given the difficulty of creating accurate analytical models for this problem, we collect and publicly release datasets to facilitate data-driven approaches. Third, we present three algorithms to autonomously drive wheeled robots over vertically challenging terrain, an open-loop, a classical rule-based, and an end-to-end learning-based approach, which can serve as baselines for benchmarking future research. We provide extensive experimental results for all three algorithms in both an indoor controlled testbed and outdoor natural environments, confirm our hypothesis, and point out future research directions for wheeled mobility on vertically challenging terrain. To the best of our knowledge, no existing work has tackled vertically challenging terrain with conventional wheeled robots in the real world.
